keyPoint.sourceEnglish: A hot centre does not prove the whole heap is sanitised
keyPoint.draft: Karolo e bohareng e chesang ha e pake hore qubu yohle e sanitised.
keyPoint.literalBacktranslation: A hot central part does not prove that the whole heap is sanitised.
keyPoint.uncertainty: Keeps sanitised in English to avoid treating heat as proof of a sanitation outcome. “Centre” is rendered as the central part; “does not prove” remains explicit.

question.sourceEnglish: A farmer's compost heap smells strongly of ammonia and is wet and slimy. What's the fix?
question.draft: Qubu ya compost ya molemi e nkha ammonia haholo mme e metsi ebile e slimy. Tharollo ke efe?
question.literalBacktranslation: The farmer's compost heap smells strongly of ammonia and is wet and slimy. What is the fix?
question.uncertainty: Retains ammonia and slimy as technical/sensory terms. Both the strong smell and wet, slimy condition remain in the question.

options.currentDraft: Eketsa disebediswa tse tala tse nang le naetrojene e ngata

options.sourceEnglish: Add more dry carbon material like straw and turn the heap
options.currentDraft: Eketsa disebediswa tse omileng tsa khabone (carbon) jwalo ka jwang bo omileng (straw) mme o phethole qubu

options.sourceEnglish: Stop turning it and let it cool
options.currentDraft: Kgaotsa ho e phethola mme o e tlohele e fole

options.sourceEnglish: Add more water — the smell means it's too dry
options.currentDraft: Eketsa metsi a mangata — monko o bolela hore e omeletse haholo

rationale.sourceEnglish: A wet, slimy heap may need more air and drier material. Add dry browns and turn the heap to open it up. An ammonia smell can also suggest too much nitrogen-rich material. Check that the heap stays damp, not soggy.
rationale.draft: Qubu e metsi, e slimy e ka hloka moya o mongata le material e ommeng ho feta. Eketsa dry browns mme o phethole qubu hore e bulehe mme moya o kene. Monko wa ammonia le wona o ka bontsha hore ho na le material e ngata haholo e nang le nitrogen. Hlahloba hore qubu e dule e le damp, e se be soggy.
rationale.literalBacktranslation: A wet, slimy heap may need more air and drier material. Add dry browns and turn the heap so it opens and air enters. An ammonia smell can also indicate that there is too much nitrogen-rich material. Check that the heap stays damp, not soggy.
rationale.uncertainty: Preserves “may need,” the action of adding dry browns and turning to open the heap, and “can also suggest” rather than asserting excess nitrogen as certain. Damp/not soggy remains an explicit condition; technical moisture and compost-category terms stay English.

question.sourceEnglish: Why keep wattle seed pods out of an ordinary compost heap?
question.currentDraft: Ke hobaneng ha o lokela ho boloka makgapha a dipeo tsa wattle kantle ho qubu e tlwaelehileng ya kompose?

options.sourceEnglish: Bark makes every heap too hot
options.currentDraft: Makgapetla a difate a etsa hore qubu e nngwe le e nngwe e tjhese haholo

options.sourceEnglish: Some seeds may survive and spread when the compost is used
options.currentDraft: Dipeo tse ding di ka nna tsa pholoha mme tsa nama ha kompose e sebediswa
Makgapha a dula a hulela mohlwa kamehla

options.sourceEnglish: Pods release a gas that kills every soil organism
options.currentDraft: Makgapha a lokolla kgase e bolayang setshedi se seng le se seng sa mobu

rationale.sourceEnglish: An ordinary heap may not expose every seed to conditions that make it non-viable. Excluding pods avoids spreading them with the compost.
rationale.draft: Qubu e tlwaelehileng e ka nna ya se pepesetse peo e nngwe le e nngwe maemong a ka e etsang hore e se hlole e kgona ho mela (non-viable). Ho ntsha makgapha a dipeo ho thibela hore a se ke a nama mmoho le kompose.
rationale.literalBacktranslation: An ordinary heap may not expose every seed to conditions that could make it no longer able to germinate (non-viable). Removing the seed pods prevents them from spreading together with the compost.
rationale.uncertainty: “May not” and “every seed” remain explicit; the wording does not claim that every seed survives or that an ordinary heap never makes seeds non-viable. Keeps the source's reason for excluding pods: avoiding their spread with compost.

semanticChecks: Quiz 0 asks about both a strong ammonia smell and a wet, slimy heap; answer index 1 remains dry carbon material such as straw plus turning.

Quiz 0 rationale: a wet, slimy heap may need more air and drier material; add dry browns and turn to open it up; ammonia smell can also suggest too much nitrogen-rich material; check damp, not soggy. No certainty claim about excess nitrogen.
Quiz 1 retains the wattle seed pod exclusion and ordinary-heap uncertainty: every seed is not necessarily exposed to conditions that make it non-viable; exclusion avoids spread with compost.
No species, quantities, timings, sanitation guarantees or other conditions were added.
uncertaintySummary: Independent semantic backcheck accepted the source meaning and preserved indices/order. This remains a machine draft, not fluent approval. Compost browns/greens, sanitation, seed viability and damp/soggy terminology remain in English where technical precision is uncertain.
